current_pob.text: Then David said to Abishai[a], “Now Sheba son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. You, take your lord’s servants and pursue after him, lest he find fortified cities for himself and escape from our sight.”

footnotes.text: Hebrew literally, 'and deliver our eyes,' an idiom meaning 'escape from our sight' or 'elude us.'

findings.observation: Pinned matza is Qal perfect 3ms, not yimtsa. GKC and Driver's following-consecutive objection is substantive and was underemphasized in the initial sample.
findings.candidate_comparison: Current 'lest he find' preserves urgency but is temporally less explicit than a possibly-accomplished reading. Diagnostic 'for fear he has already found' foregrounds anteriority but makes 'already' explicit and may overstate a disputed interpretation. 'Before he finds' narrows it further to prospective prevention. None is approved as the best full-verse replacement.
findings.strongest_counterargument: Fear clauses are modal and need not map word-for-word to English tense; a feared completed scenario may still motivate urgent pursuit. Conversely the following consecutive supplies a concrete reason to suspect lost yod.
findings.confidence: High morphology and accurate scholarship attribution; moderate unresolved temporal interpretation; no demonstrated textual priority.

findings.observation: Pinned wehitzil is Hiphil of natsal; the eye is its object, not an explicit from-phrase. Driver/BDB gloss the local noun singular. Greek and Syriac editions use plural eyes.
findings.candidate_comparison: Escape/elusion and serious injury can both be interpretations of the retained removal expression; they are not automatically different Hebrew source texts. A shadow derivation requires separate morphological/repointing adjudication. Niphal escape plus mimmennu is a different Hebrew proposal, not an English synonym for the existing pointed sequence.
findings.strongest_counterargument: The pursuit, fortified refuge and eventual siege make practical evasion coherent. Literal eye injury can function as a severe-harm metaphor, so the versions do not force new consonants. Neither reading is grammatically transparent enough to erase uncertainty.
findings.confidence: High consulted version wording; moderate local metaphor; low historical-priority determination.

findings.strongest_counterargument: The current expression is understandable and retains a visible correspondence to the Hebrew directional phrase; this is a small naturalness gain, not recovered meaning.

findings.proposal: Move the existing note anchor from Abishai to the final phrase; replace the settled-idiom claim with: Hebrew, 'and take away our eye'; the expression is uncertain. 'Escape from our sight' is one interpretation.
findings.strongest_counterargument: An uncertainty note adds reader burden to a contextually plausible established rendering; nonetheless its current anchor misidentifies the subject of the note and its certainty outruns the evidence.

findings.observation: Pinned Hebrew names Abishai; consulted Greek has Abessa while consulted Syriac names Joab.
findings.strongest_counterargument: Joab could reflect a different source or adjustment to the surrounding Joab-led action. Versional genealogy and Hebrew coverage are uncollated. No name change is authorized.
